planting.note: Grow as a houseplant or shaded, humid patio container in bright, indirect light in a loose, well-drained epiphytic bromeliad mix; scarlet star is frost-tender and grown outdoors year-round only in zones 10-11.

directions: Grow as a houseplant or shaded, humid patio container in bright, indirect light in a loose, well-drained epiphytic bromeliad mix; scarlet star is frost-tender and grown outdoors year-round only in zones 10-11. Rather than a showy flower spike, this striking bromeliad puts on its display through its foliage: the central leaves of the rosette flush a brilliant blood-red to orange at bloom time, surrounding small, inconspicuous true flowers hidden at the base, a foliar 'flower' effect that persists far longer than typical bromeliad blooms. Native to Central and South American rainforests, where it grows as an epiphyte on tree branches, it appreciates high humidity and bright, filtered light rather than direct sun, and like other guzmanias should be kept with a small reservoir of water in its central cup, refreshed regularly to prevent stagnation. After flowering the rosette gradually declines, having produced offset pups at its base that can be separated and grown on to continue the planting.

planting.note: Plant container-grown shrubs in spring in lean, sandy to rocky, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; locustberry is frost-tender and native to the pine rockland and coastal habitats of extreme South Florida and the Keys.

directions: Plant container-grown shrubs in spring in lean, sandy to rocky, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; locustberry is frost-tender and native to the pine rockland and coastal habitats of extreme South Florida and the Keys. Small, glossy, leathery leaves and delicate clusters of small flowers that open pink and fade to yellow give this native shrub extended seasonal interest, followed by small red berries that ripen to nearly black and are eaten by birds, while the foliage serves as a larval host plant for several native butterfly species. Highly tolerant of poor, rocky limestone soil, salt exposure, and drought once established, it is a valuable, low-maintenance shrub for a South Florida native landscape, coastal planting, or pollinator garden, requiring essentially no irrigation or fertilizer beyond its first year. Prune lightly to shape if a more formal habit is wanted, though it naturally maintains an attractive, open form without regular pruning.

planting.note: Plant container-grown trees in spring in lean, rocky, well-drained, alkaline soil in full sun; lignum vitae is frost-tender, extremely slow-growing, and native to South Florida hammocks and the Keys.

directions: Plant container-grown trees in spring in lean, rocky, well-drained, alkaline soil in full sun; lignum vitae is frost-tender, extremely slow-growing, and native to South Florida hammocks and the Keys. Small, leathery, evergreen leaflets cover a dense, rounded canopy that bursts into a profusion of vivid blue-purple flowers, often several times a year, followed by bright yellow-orange seed capsules that split to reveal striking red-coated seeds, making it one of the most ornamentally distinctive native trees of South Florida. Its extremely dense, heavy wood — historically the source of the actual lignum vitae timber prized for its self-lubricating properties in ship propeller shaft bearings — reflects an exceptionally slow growth rate that has made wild populations vulnerable to historical overharvesting, so cultivated specimens from nursery-propagated stock help support the species. Extremely drought- and salt-tolerant once established, it thrives on poor, rocky, alkaline soil with essentially no supplemental care, making it a valuable, low-maintenance native specimen tree for a South Florida landscape.

planting.note: Plant container-grown trees in spring in well-drained, sandy to rocky soil in full sun; Jamaica dogwood is frost-tender and native to coastal hammocks of South Florida, the Keys, and the wider Caribbean basin.

directions: Plant container-grown trees in spring in well-drained, sandy to rocky soil in full sun; Jamaica dogwood is frost-tender and native to coastal hammocks of South Florida, the Keys, and the wider Caribbean basin. A member of the legume family, this fast-growing native tree produces showy clusters of pink-and-white, pea-shaped flowers in spring before new leaves emerge, followed by distinctive four-winged seed pods, and its bark and roots contain compounds historically used by Caribbean fishers to stun fish, giving the tree its 'fishpoison' common name — a traditional practice not appropriate or legal for casual use today. Highly salt- and wind-tolerant, it is well suited to coastal landscaping in South Florida, tolerating the sandy, well-drained soils and salt spray of shoreline plantings with little supplemental care once established. Water regularly while young, and provide the full sun and coastal exposure this tough, fast-growing native tree tolerates well in its home range.

planting.note: Plant container-grown shrubs in spring in well-drained, sandy to rocky soil in partial shade to full sun; rough velvetseed is frost-tender and native to coastal hammocks and pinelands of South Florida.

directions: Plant container-grown shrubs in spring in well-drained, sandy to rocky soil in partial shade to full sun; rough velvetseed is frost-tender and native to coastal hammocks and pinelands of South Florida. Rough, sandpaper-textured leaves cover a large shrub or small tree bearing small, fragrant, white to cream flowers followed by red berries that turn black as they ripen, providing food for a range of native birds and wildlife across its hammock and coastal scrub habitat. Well adapted to the poor, well-drained, often rocky limestone soils typical of South Florida's native plant communities, it tolerates both dry, sunny sites and the partial shade of a hammock understory, making it a versatile choice for naturalistic native landscaping. It needs little supplemental water or fertilizer once established and provides good wildlife habitat value with minimal maintenance.

planting.note: Plant container-grown shrubs in spring in well-drained, sandy to loamy soil in partial shade to full sun; Guianese colicwood tolerates a range of soil moisture from dry to seasonally wet.

directions: Plant container-grown shrubs in spring in well-drained, sandy to loamy soil in partial shade to full sun; Guianese colicwood tolerates a range of soil moisture from dry to seasonally wet. Small, leathery, dark green leaves densely clothe an upright, multi-trunked native shrub or small tree, with inconspicuous flowers followed by small, dark purple-black berries that provide reliable food for native birds through much of the year. Native to hammocks, pinelands, and wetland edges across Florida and the Caribbean basin, it is an adaptable, low-maintenance understory shrub tolerant of both dry and periodically moist soils, useful for a hedge, screen, or wildlife habitat planting in a native landscape. It handles both sun and considerable shade well, and needs only routine watering during establishment before becoming largely self-sufficient.
